item.title: Popcorn Time Updater Left Millions of PCs Open to Whoever Owned Its Dead Web Addresses
item.description:
Up to 3 million Windows PCs and 350,000 Macs kept asking dead web addresses for updates to a movie app from 2014. The owners did nothing wrong. The updater had the highest rights and ran whatever came back.

Then a security company registered those addresses and found out what they meant. Over the months that followed, it sent its own code to those computers more than 2 million times, on machines that were not its own.

Maybe you remember Popcorn Time. It came out in 2014 and let you stream films over BitTorrent. The original project shut down that same year, but copies carried on under other names. One of them, Time4Popcorn, was closed source, and its makers also handed it out as Popcorn Time. Maybe you installed it once, for one film, and never thought about it again. Its makers abandoned it. On millions of computers it stayed installed anyway, together with a small helper program that kept running in the background long after the film app itself was forgotten.

That helper turned up when researchers at Eye Security searched a customer’s network for signs of attackers, a job called a threat hunt. On a laptop, a process called Updater.exe kept trying to reach the address popcorntimeupd.xyz, and that domain was no longer registered. So they registered it themselves, to see what would show up. About 50 requests per second came in. That is more than 4 million a day.

Each request looked like this:

1

GET /?app_id=T4PSEC&hid=...&ver=6.1.0.0&os=WIN060200

The computer told the server which app it belonged to and gave a hardware ID for that one machine. It also sent a version number and the version of Windows it was running. It kept sending that to an address that had stopped being registered.

Over six months they saw around 3.8 million different hardware IDs. Some of those IDs were wrong, in two directions. A bug in the Windows updater left out the one value that is unique to each PC, so laptops cloned from the same disk image all ended up with one shared ID. Many PCs counted as one. On a Mac the ID most likely changed whenever the hostname changed, so one Mac could show up many times.

After correcting for that, they landed on 2.5 to 3 million Windows computers and 250,000 to 350,000 Macs. Android made up less than 5 percent.

The updater asked the address whether there was a new version. The question and the answer travelled over plain HTTP, so without encryption. The answer was a short JSON message, a few lines of text that pointed to a program. The updater downloaded that program and started it, and because the updates carried no signature, it never checked who had made what it was about to run. The Mac version expected a very different JSON message.

And owning the domain was only one way in. Because the traffic was not encrypted, the researchers’ own security advisory warns that whoever can tamper with it on the way can slip in an update of their own. On a hacked router or a fake WiFi hotspot, the request can be answered by someone in between, no matter who owns the domain.

On Windows, Updater.exe runs as a service under NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. That is the Windows account with more rights than an administrator, more than you have yourself when you log in. On a Mac, PT.updd runs as root, the Mac account with full control. On both it works in the background, and you see nothing. Whoever controls the answer can run any program on your computer.

The flaw now has a public ID, CVE-2026-30612. CISA, the US cyber agency, rates it 9.8 out of 10. It covers the Windows versions up to 6.2.1.18, macOS up to 6.2.1.17 and Android up to 3.5.0.173.

Android works differently, because it has no background updater. The app checks for a new version when you open it and then asks whether you want to install it. An attacker who controls the answer can still put their own app in front of you, and you only have to tap yes.

The requests came from home internet connections around the world. They also came from company networks, and from government and military networks. Many of the people behind those computers, the researchers think, had forgotten about the software years ago and were no longer using it. It was a film app someone installed once, still running with the highest rights on the machine.

Normally you warn the maker of the software. Here there was no maker to call. The researchers called the people behind the app pirates, and asked what those pirates could have done about it even if they had reached them. The only party that could close the hole was whoever held the address, and that was now them. Doing nothing, they wrote, would not make the world any better.

They compare what they were about to do with the police action against Emotet. In January 2021, police took over that botnet and pushed an update through its own channel to the computers it had infected. On April 25, 2021, that update removed the malware. It only deleted the malware’s Windows services and its autorun registry key, then stopped, and left everything else on the machine alone. One difference they point out themselves: the Popcorn Time users probably installed the software on purpose, where that botnet’s malware got onto computers without asking.

So they sent an update of their own. On Windows it stopped the service called Update service and switched it off. On a Mac it unloaded the background task that starts PT.updd. It collected no data and deleted no files. They started small. At first only machines they had already seen got the update, each ID got it a single time, and where possible they moved the connection over to HTTPS. After a few weeks they dropped those limits.

They began sending it in November 2025, and by December more than 1 million systems had it. A few weeks in, the requests had dropped by 90 percent. By March 1, 2026 they were down by 98 percent, though about 5,000 updates a day were still going out. In total, machines downloaded it more than 2 million times. In late March they handed their 15 domains to The Shadowserver Foundation. They published the advisory on June 11, 2026, and presented the full operation at the Hack.lu conference on October 22, 2026.

Antivirus products flagged their fix as malware, and from the outside it did look like malware: a program pushed over plain HTTP that started itself on computers that never asked for it. So they changed their code until the scanners stopped catching it. By their own count, one vendor still detects it.

In 2023, a French security company ended up in almost the same position. It paid 7 dollars for the IP address of a server that a self-spreading worm called PlugX still reported to. Between 90,000 and 100,000 unique addresses checked in each day, and more than 2.5 million over six months, from more than 170 countries.

The worm even had a built-in command to delete itself. The company did not send it. It wrote that sending commands to other people’s machines raised legal problems, so it left that decision to the police and national cyber teams in each country. French police then led the cleanup, with the company’s help. In the US, the FBI needed nine court warrants to delete the worm from about 4,258 computers, and the last one expired on January 3, 2025. Afterwards, the agency let the owners know through their internet providers.

The researchers’ writeup mentions no police or warrant for this operation, and no message to the owners. One line says their own legal team gave some advice, without saying what that advice was. So a company decided for itself to run code on more than 2 million computers it did not own. Those computers are safer because of it. And if one of them was yours, the writeup gives no sign that you were ever told. Who gets to make that call is still an open question.

Their fix only switched off the updater. It did not remove the app, and the app itself is still unsafe. It runs on a Chrome engine from 2014 with the sandbox turned off, the part of a browser that keeps a web page away from the rest of your system.

The app also loads parts of its code over plain HTTP from abandoned domains, and the researchers showed that this route can start a program on the computer. Some of the old Popcorn Time domains are still in the hands of third parties. On Android they could not switch the updater off at all, because it sits inside the app.

The official CVE record for the flaw, published on August 27, 2026, points its exploit link to a page about a WiFi router from a different company. That page has nothing to do with Popcorn Time. The record does not link to the researchers’ own advisory either.

Since early 2025, a new project has been using the Popcorn Time name to build a legal alternative, and that is separate software. The research here is about Time4Popcorn, the copy that was also handed out under the Popcorn Time name.

If you ever installed it, this is where the updater sits:

  • → Windows: C:\Program Files\Popcorn Time\Updater.exe or C:\Program Files (x86)\Popcorn Time\Updater.exe
  • → Mac: /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools/PT.updd
  • → Android: inside the app itself

On Windows you can see whether the service still exists and whether it runs:

1

sc.exe query "Update service"

On a Mac, this shows whether the helper is still on the disk:

1

ls -l /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools/PT.updd

The advice from the researchers is short: uninstall it. If you cannot do that right away, these commands from their advisory switch off the updater. On Windows, in a command prompt opened as administrator:

1
2

sc.exe stop "Update service"
sc.exe config "Update service" start= disabled

On a Mac, in Terminal with administrator rights:

1

launchctl unload -w /Library/LaunchDaemons/PT.updd.plist

On Android, remove the app, because there the updater cannot be switched off.

If you look after a network, the researchers published the domains and files to hunt for. They also ask security vendors to flag Updater.exe and PT.updd as potentially unwanted programs, so the helper gets caught on machines where the owner forgot it was ever installed.

A program you stopped using can keep running with the highest rights on your computer, asking an address on the internet what to run next. Whoever owns that address decides what your computer does.

Could you open Wireshark on your own computer and see which program calls home over plain HTTP, and what it pulls down?

item.title: FreeCell From 1993 Still Runs Unchanged on Windows 11 (1993)
item.description:
A file from 1993 opens on a fully updated Windows 11 in 2026 and plays like nothing ever changed. It is FreeCell, the card game, 33 years old. What makes it run is the same reason dangerous old code lingers in Windows.

The program is FREECELL.EXE, and the copy that still works is the one that shipped with Win32s, an add-on from 1993 that let early 32-bit software run on Windows 3.1. The file was built on July 4, 1993. It is 49,188 bytes. Copy it and its own CARDS.DLL onto a Windows 11 machine, double-click, and the green table with the four free cells in the corner opens.

Win32s itself was a temporary measure. In 1993 the computer on an ordinary desk still ran Windows 3.1, which was a 16-bit system, and Microsoft wanted to give developers a way to start writing the 32-bit software that Windows NT and later Windows 95 would need. Win32s was that link, a set of extra files added to Windows 3.1 that translated 32-bit calls down to the 16-bit system underneath. FreeCell came along with it, and because it was built as a proper 32-bit program, it is the same kind of program Windows 11 still runs today.

I read the file itself instead of trusting the story. Inside, the description still says “Entertainment Pack FreeCell Game,” with the line “Copyright © Microsoft Corp. 1981-1993.” It asks Windows for five things and no more: KERNEL32, USER32, GDI32, SHELL32, and its own CARDS.DLL, the small library that draws the deck. The first four are core Windows files, and they are sitting on your machine right now, under the same names, doing the same work they did in 1993.

That is the reason it still opens. A 32-bit program like this one reaches a 64-bit machine through a translator called WOW64, which Microsoft describes as the x86 emulator that lets 32-bit Windows applications run on 64-bit Windows. WOW64 comes with the system and is always present. It keeps the old program and the modern one apart, hands FreeCell the 1993-era interfaces it expects, and translates between the two. The game has no idea it is running on a 64-bit machine.

Where Windows keeps all of this holds a joke. The 64-bit system files sit in a folder called System32, and the 32-bit ones, the kind FreeCell needs, sit in a folder called SysWOW64. The names look backwards, and they are, kept that way on purpose so that old programs looking for System32 would still find what they expected. FreeCell asks for its four Windows libraries, Windows quietly points it at the 32-bit copies in SysWOW64, and the game never notices the switch.

What it cannot do is go back one more step. Windows 11 is 64-bit only, and 64-bit Windows does not run 16-bit programs at all. Microsoft gives a plain reason for that line. Windows keeps track of open windows and files with small numbers called handles, and on a 64-bit system those numbers are too large to hand to a 16-bit program without losing part of them. Try to launch a 16-bit application and Windows stops with one error, ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT.

So the games from the first Windows, like Reversi from 1985, will not start on their own. Windows 11 cannot run them without help. You need something like otvdm, a free and open-source tool that imitates that old 16-bit world, or a virtual machine with an old Windows inside it. otvdm is a community project, a reworked version of an older 16-bit Windows emulator, ported to 64-bit Windows. The person who went hunting for the oldest Windows program that still runs called leaning on it “cheating,” and that is fair. Reversi needs that crutch. FreeCell does not.

Between those two sits an even older survivor. A CD player program linked in November 1992, from an early test build of Windows NT, still runs on Windows 11 as well. It works because of one file, crtdll.dll, an early Microsoft C runtime library from that time. Windows 11 still ships it, tucked into SysWOW64 where the 32-bit pieces live. The 1992 program asks for that file by name, finds one exactly where it expects, and runs.

And then, in late March 2026, that forgotten file caused a mess. A Windows 11 update replaced crtdll.dll with a different library that did not hold the same functions inside. Users who looked closely reported the file’s version had jumped from 4.0.1183.1, a number from the 1990s, to 10.0.26100.8115, a modern Windows build, and that the replacement sent programs to a different runtime than the one they were written for. Old 32-bit programs that leaned on it stopped starting. People who still used decades-old tools noticed within days. One wrote, “I still use this app and it has always worked until today,” after Cardfile, the index-card program that came with Windows from version 1.01 up to NT 4.0, suddenly refused to open. These are reports from users on Microsoft’s own forums, not an official notice. On April 14, the Patch Tuesday update put the old version of the file back. The game keeps running because Microsoft almost never touches these pieces, and when it did, things broke within days.

This is a choice, and Microsoft has made it for a long time. Raymond Chen, an engineer who has written about the inside of Windows for over twenty years, once told a story that captures it. A popular MS-DOS game from 1994 refused to run on Windows 95 if the computer had more than 16 megabytes of memory. The game was written for an older processor that could not count past that. Microsoft fixed it on its own side. It built a setting into Windows for that one game that said, in Chen’s words, “Never give this program more than 16MB of memory.” As he put it, the game then ran better under Windows 95 than it did under plain MS-DOS, where it would have crashed. Multiply that by thousands of programs across decades, and you get the Windows you use now, an operating system that carries its past with it so that almost nothing ever written stops working.

That is a gift if you depend on old software. It is also a problem, because code that never leaves is still there for an attacker to abuse. The parts Windows keeps for the sake of the past can also be used, and some of them have been.

The clearest example is the modem drivers. For years Windows shipped with drivers for Agere soft modems, the dial-up hardware that few people have owned since the 2000s. The hardware was gone, but the drivers stayed, loaded and trusted, on fully updated machines. Then researchers found a flaw in one of them, ltmdm64.sys, tracked as CVE-2025-24990. Microsoft’s own advisory says attackers were already using it, and that it let them gain administrator rights on the machine. It reached all supported versions of Windows, Microsoft notes, even when no modem was in use, because the driver was simply there.

In October 2025 Microsoft removed the driver from Windows instead of patching it. Three months later, in January 2026, it did the same with a second Agere modem driver, agrsm64.sys, CVE-2023-31096, which could hand an attacker full SYSTEM control, the highest level on a Windows machine. That second flaw had been public since October 2023. The driver sat inside Windows for more than two years after the way to abuse it was out in the open, until Microsoft finally pulled it out.

The modems were hardware. The deeper version of this lives in a feature built for the exact purpose that keeps FreeCell running: making old software work on new Windows. It is called application compatibility, and Windows lets an administrator install fixes, called shims, that sit between a program and the system and change how the two talk. Microsoft ships a tool for it, sdbinst.exe, that registers these fixes so Windows applies them each time the program starts. It is meant for a company with an old in-house program that would otherwise break. Windows stores a shim as a small database file, an .sdb, and keeps a record of which ones it has registered. The database that comes with Windows, sysmain.sdb, holds its built-in fixes for old programs and belongs there. The worry is a custom database the owner never created, because a registered shim runs quietly and early, and installing one needs administrator rights.

Attackers worked out that the same mechanism is a quiet place to hide. A shim loads automatically and early, each time its target program runs, which is what someone who has broken into a machine wants for staying power. The public catalog of attacker techniques kept by MITRE lists this plainly. It names groups and malware that have used it to keep their access and climb to higher rights, among them FIN7, ShimRat, Pillowmint and SDBbot. Some shims can switch off protections Windows leans on, like the one that stops code from running in memory it should not. Others can slip past the permission box Windows shows before a program is given more power. The feature that keeps a 1993 card game alive is the same one that lets a break-in survive a reboot.

You can look at this on your own machine, and you do not need anything beyond what Windows already has. Windows records the registered fixes in the registry, under AppCompatFlags, and that record points to where each database actually sits. The AppPatch folder in your Windows directory is the usual spot, but a custom database can live in any folder, so the registry entry is the thing to follow. A home machine normally has the standard system database and nothing custom. If you find a custom shim database you never set up, that is one to look into, and Microsoft’s own sdbinst tool is what removes it, with sdbinst -u and the file. On a normal personal computer there is rarely a reason for a custom one to exist.

A card game from 1993 still deals its first hand on Windows 11 because Microsoft decided, long ago, that the past should keep working. That decision is why your old programs still run, and it is why the oldest corners of Windows deserve your attention, on the good days and the bad ones.

Could you list the compatibility fixes registered on your own Windows, and spot any you never set up yourself?

The game has no idea it is running on a 64-bit machine.

Where Windows keeps all of this holds a joke. The 64-bit system files sit in a folder called System32, and the 32-bit ones, the kind FreeCell needs, sit in a folder called SysWOW64. The names look backwards, and they are, kept that way on purpose so that old programs looking for System32 would still find what they expected. FreeCell asks for its four Windows libraries, Windows quietly points it at the 32-bit copies in SysWOW64, and the game never notices the switch.

What it cannot do is go back one more step. Windows 11 is 64-bit only, and 64-bit Windows does not run 16-bit programs at all. Microsoft gives a plain reason for that line. Windows keeps track of open windows and files with small numbers called handles, and on a 64-bit system those numbers are too large to hand to a 16-bit program without losing part of them. Try to launch a 16-bit application and Windows stops with one error, ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT.

So the games from the first Windows, like Reversi from 1985, will not start on their own. Windows 11 cannot run them without help. You need something like otvdm, a free and open-source tool that imitates that old 16-bit world, or a virtual machine with an old Windows inside it. otvdm is a community project, a reworked version of an older 16-bit Windows emulator, ported to 64-bit Windows. Between those two sits an even older survivor. A CD player program linked in November 1992, from an early test build of Windows NT, still runs on Windows 11 as well. And then, in late March 2026, that forgotten file caused a mess. A Windows 11 update replaced crtdll.dll with a different library that did not hold the same functions inside. One wrote, “I still use this app and it has always worked until today,” after Cardfile, the index-card program that came with Windows from version 1.01 up to NT 4.0, suddenly refused to open. These are reports from users on Microsoft’s own forums, not an official notice. On April 14, the Patch Tuesday update put the old version of the file back. The game keeps running because Microsoft almost never touches these pieces, and when it did, things broke within days.

This is a choice, and Microsoft has made it for a long time. Raymond Chen, an engineer who has written about the inside of Windows for over twenty years, once told a story that captures it. Multiply that by thousands of programs across decades, and you get the Windows you use now, an operating system that carries its past with it so that almost nothing ever written stops working.

That is a gift if you depend on old software. It is also a problem, because code that never leaves is still there for an attacker to abuse. The parts Windows keeps for the sake of the past can also be used, and some of them have been.

The clearest example is the modem drivers. For years Windows shipped with drivers for Agere soft modems, the dial-up hardware that few people have owned since the 2000s. The modems were hardware. The deeper version of this lives in a feature built for the exact purpose that keeps FreeCell running: making old software work on new Windows. It is called application compatibility, and Windows lets an administrator install fixes, called shims, that sit between a program and the system and change how the two talk. It is meant for a company with an old in-house program that would otherwise break. Windows stores a shim as a small database file, an .sdb, and keeps a record of which ones it has registered. The database that comes with Windows, sysmain.sdb, holds its built-in fixes for old programs and belongs there. The worry is a custom database the owner never created, because a registered shim runs quietly and early, and installing one needs administrator rights.

Attackers worked out that the same mechanism is a quiet place to hide. item.title: NFC Relay Scam Took €380,000 From About 170 Bank Customers in Three Weeks
item.description:
About 170 people held their bank card against their own phone and lost €380,000 in three weeks. Dozens were in their 20s and 30s. An app sent the chip to an ATM. Czechia, Russia, Italy and Brazil saw it first.

The call began with a recorded voice, made with AI. A phone rang somewhere in the Netherlands, and the message said there was suspicious activity on the bank account. The message asked for a 1 on the keypad if that activity was unfamiliar. Those who pressed 1 heard music for a while, and then someone came on the line who said they worked for the bank.

That person had a story ready. The bank card had to be blocked, and it had to happen quickly, before more money disappeared. To block it, the customer had to download an app and hold the card against the phone so the app could scan it.

The scammers had made dozens of different audio fragments with AI, with different voices, banks, companies and scenarios, ready for whoever picked up. The victims came from across the country and were of all ages, the police say, with dozens of people in their twenties and thirties among them.

While the card was held against the phone, an accomplice with the same app stood at a cash machine somewhere else, waiting. The police call this person the pinner. Thousands of euros came out of those machines while the people on the phone still believed they were blocking their card.

The cybercrime team of the Rotterdam police counted about 170 victims and €380,000 in damage on the group’s servers, over three weeks. The case began in mid-September 2026, when Dutch banks reported a new form of bank helpdesk fraud through the Electronic Crimes Task Force, where banks, the police and the Public Prosecution Service work together. Ruben van Well of the cybercrime team said the police had not come across this technical method before. He described the scammer in this case as a convincing caller who comes across as very professional.

A bank card has a small chip inside it that can talk by radio, but only over a very short distance. That is NFC, near field communication, and it is what makes contactless payment work. When a card is held against a payment terminal or a cash machine, the machine sends the chip a series of short commands and the chip answers each one. Those commands and answers are called APDUs. The chip answers any reader held close to it, and a phone with NFC can be that reader.

The app the victims installed read the card the way a payment terminal would, and then it did one more thing. It sent the card’s answers over the internet to a second phone.

That second phone was in the pinner’s hand at the cash machine, and it presented itself to the machine as the victim’s card. When the machine sent a command, that command traveled over the internet to the victim’s phone and on to the card. The card’s answer traveled back the same way to the machine. This is called NFC relay, and the card never left the victim’s hand. The chip makes a new one-time security code for each contactless payment, so the card has to answer live, at the moment of the withdrawal. That is why the pinner stood at the machine at the same time.

The chip alone does not get cash out of a Dutch machine. Contactless withdrawal at Geldmaat, the Dutch cash machine network, has been possible since October 3, 2023, and the PIN still has to be typed in at the machine. So the pinner needed the PIN as well.

The Dutch police have not said how the scammers got the PIN in this case. Their warning does name it: a bank will never ask you to download an app, hold your bank card against your phone, or give your PIN. In earlier cases of this trick in other countries, the PIN came from the victim. The app asked for it, or the caller did, as part of what was presented as a check.

The trick was first found in Czechia. From November 2023, a group there used fake banking apps to steal the login details of customers of three Czech banks, and in March 2024 it added a second app for the card. Victims got a text message about a tax refund with a link to the fake banking app. After they logged in, someone called them posing as their bank, said their account had been compromised, and sent a link to that second app. It asked for their client number, date of birth and PIN, and then told them to hold their card against the phone until it was recognized. Their phones did not have to be rooted. Because the victims had already typed their banking login into the fake app, the attackers could also change the withdrawal limits on their accounts. When a cash withdrawal failed, they could still move the money to other bank accounts.

ESET, the security company that found the malware and named it NGate, published its analysis in August 2024. The malware was built on NFCGate, a research tool made by students at the Technical University of Darmstadt in Germany. In March 2024, Czech police arrested a 22-year-old who had been taking money out of cash machines in Prague. He had 160,000 Czech koruna on him, more than €6,000, and the police said that money came from only the last three victims.

After that, NFC relay spread to other countries, and the same company measured more than 35 times as many NFC attacks in the first half of 2025 as in the second half of 2024. In the six months after that, its numbers went up by another 87 percent.

In Russia, police detained the developer and the main administrator of one of these tools in December 2025. The preliminary damage was more than 200 million rubles. Victims there were told to hold their card against their phone and type their PIN for a fake authorization.

In Italy, bank customers were hit by SuperCard X, which the security company Cleafy exposed in April 2025. It was run by Chinese-speaking criminals who rented the tool out to others.

By October 2025, the mobile security company Zimperium had counted more than 760 malicious apps of this kind, found since April 2024, with more than 70 command servers and download sites behind them. About 20 banks and other institutions had been impersonated, in countries including Russia, Poland, Czechia, Slovakia and Brazil.

In April 2026, ESET described a new version of NGate in Brazil, active since around November 2025 and hidden inside HandyPay, a legitimate app for relaying NFC payments. Victims got it through a fake lottery website and a fake Google Play page for an app that promised to protect their card. It steals the PIN and sends it to the attackers, and the researchers found signs that the malicious code was written with help from generative AI.

A month later, the company behind the SuperCard X research described two more families. DevilNFC came from Spanish-speaking criminals and impersonated a Spanish bank. NFCMultiPay was built by a Portuguese-speaking developer, most likely in Brazil. Both collect the card’s PIN as a fixed step, and both showed signs of code written with AI. After the first tap, DevilNFC asks for the PIN and sends it in plain text, together with the name of the bank and the victim’s IP address, to the attackers’ server and to a Telegram bot. Then it shows a fake verification error, so the victim holds the card against the phone for another 10 seconds and the relay gets more time. The company’s conclusion was that local groups have stopped buying these tools from Chinese-speaking sellers and now build their own.

A related method works with card details that were already stolen. ThreatFabric named it Ghost Tap in November 2024. The stolen card is loaded into Apple Pay or Google Pay on one phone, and its NFC signal is relayed to helpers who pay with it in shops. The person running it can sit in a different country. The same researchers explain why a bank has trouble spotting it. The payments appear to come from the same device, a single payment can stay below the amount that triggers a check, and the phone with the stolen card on it can be in airplane mode. In August 2025, Recorded Future reported that Chinese-speaking groups use this for cash machine withdrawals and for buying jewelry and phones, which they sell for cash through Telegram channels. Some of these groups work only within China, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines, and the researchers wrote that these campaigns can be run on a global scale. In Singapore the method became widely known through high-profile arrests.

Bank helpdesk fraud itself is not new in the Netherlands. In 2025 it hit slightly fewer than 5,900 people and cost €25.8 million, according to the yearly fraud figures of the Dutch banks. A little over 45 percent of that damage to private customers was paid back by the banks as a goodwill gesture. This one group made about 170 victims in three weeks.

On October 15, 2026, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled on a phishing case from Poland. A bank customer had lost about €700 after entering her login details on a fake copy of her bank’s website. Her bank refused to pay it back, because it said she had been grossly negligent. The court ruled that a bank has to refund an unauthorized payment immediately, at the latest by the end of the business day after it noticed or was told about the payment. The customer has to report it without undue delay. The only exception is when the bank has reasonable grounds to suspect fraud by the customer and reports those grounds to the authorities. A bank that believes the customer was grossly negligent can try to get the money back afterwards.

The police advice:

  • → A bank never asks you to download an app, hold your bank card against your phone, or give your PIN
  • → When a call does not feel right, hang up and look at the number that called you
  • → Do not install apps from a link in a text message or a WhatsApp message
  • → In case of doubt, call your bank yourself on the number from its own website
  • → After it happened, contact your bank at once to check whether money was taken and to block the account or stop transactions if needed, report it to the police, and keep the messages as evidence

On October 6, the police arrested two men. According to the police, a technician and a coordinator were responsible for the technology and for sending out the fake calls. A 23-year-old from Vaassen is suspected of handling the technical side of the fraud and directing others. A 25-year-old from Ede is suspected of a coordinating role. The police took the group’s servers offline and are going through that data, along with the phones and laptops they seized. On October 20, the court decided that both men stay in custody for another 90 days while they wait for their trial. Neither of them has been convicted, and the police have not said whether AI played any part in building the app.

The Rotterdam investigator also said that pinners are easy to replace.

In Czechia in early 2024, it started with a text message about a tax refund. In the Netherlands in September 2026, it started with an AI voice. The step that got the money out stayed the same: a bank card held against a phone.

In a lab on your own laptop, you can clone a login page and watch what a victim types into it. item.title: Lenovo ThinkPlus Fingerprint USB Drive Sold as Encrypted Was a Plain SD Card Inside
item.description:
USB encryption from five makers opened without the password. Lenovo, Netac, KakaSoft, Nexcopy, SecZure. A Lenovo USB stick with a fingerprint reader was sold as hardware encrypted with AES-256. Inside sat an ordinary SD card. Nothing on it was encrypted. The fingerprint only switched the USB connection on.

The stick is the ThinkPlus FU100, a small black stick with a fingerprint sensor on top that opens with a finger or a password. It is marketed as hardware encrypted with AES-256, and a sales listing promises fingerprint protection, password protection and anti-leakage. Someone who bought one to carry private files had good reason to believe the fingerprint locked those files.

Xusheng Li develops a reverse engineering tool and its debugger. In 2025 he took an FU100 apart. Under the plastic was a small circuit board with an SD card on it. The data on that card was not encrypted in any way. The fingerprint reader decided one thing: whether the stick connected to the computer or stayed silent. The files on the card did not depend on it. Lenovo later described the flaw in its own advisory as a weakness that lets someone with physical access read the data stored on the drive.

He reported it to Lenovo on August 2, 2025. On August 27 a temporary fix was ready. It was a layer of epoxy over the SD card. A proper fix was planned for December.

The FU100 was the first case in a talk he gave in March 2026 at RE//verse, a conference for reverse engineers. One of his first slides said: do not trust encrypted USB drives, check what the vendor claims yourself.

The second Lenovo device was the ThinkPlus TSD303, an external SSD that also opens with a fingerprint or a password. Inside is a standard M.2 SSD, and here the data is encrypted. The weak point was the password. When the Lenovo program on the computer asked the drive for it, the drive sent the correct password back over the USB cable in plain text. The program then compared it with what the user typed. On his slide, the captured USB packet shows his test password in the last bytes, readable as text. Whoever could watch that traffic, or the memory of that program, could read the password and open the drive with it.

Three months after his report, Lenovo sent him a fix to test. In that version the drive sent an encrypted blob where the plain password used to be, and at first he took it for a hash of the password. He traced it back with the debugger. The blob came from SM4, a block cipher similar to AES, and its key was derived from something that looked like a timestamp. In his test that key was 2021012700000000. He fed the blob and that key into a decryption tool, and his test password came out. The fix was incomplete, because the program could derive the key, and so could someone who took the program apart.

His slide lists ten devices built on the same software kit, with the vendor names blacked out. The TSD303 is one of them, and the slide notes that other vendors using the kit are affected in the same way. Six of those devices sent the password in plain text. Two stored the data unencrypted on a micro SD card. Two sent the password with AES encryption that still gave it away.

The official description of the talk names one more brand among the devices he researched: Lexar, with its F35 Pro fingerprint stick. item.description:
An attacker drained 6.36 billion dollars from Binance in about 20 minutes across ten blockchains. No customer did anything wrong. The way in was one engineer’s laptop, rehearsed hours before.

Crypto theft has produced some huge numbers over the years, but nothing like this.

On the evening of October 29, someone reached into Binance, the largest crypto exchange there is, and walked out with 6.36 billion dollars. It took about twenty minutes, across ten different blockchains at the same time.

The people whose coins were sitting on Binance did nothing wrong.

The old record for a crypto theft was the Bybit hack in February 2025, which took 1.5 billion. This is more than four times bigger, and it is now the largest crypto theft ever recorded. When the news broke, Bitcoin dropped to a six-week low and Ether fell more than 3 percent. The market felt it.

Pulling this off is not what you would picture.

Binance keeps part of its coins in what the industry calls a hot wallet, a wallet that stays connected to the internet so the exchange can move money the moment a customer deposits or withdraws. Before any money leaves that wallet, an internal system has to sign the transaction, which is what tells the blockchain the payment really comes from Binance. That signing system is what the attacker reached. Once he had it, he could make it approve payments to himself.

Binance’s first explanation was short. The break-in, it said, may have started with a compromised laptop belonging to one of its DevOps engineers, the people who keep the exchange’s machines running. From that laptop the attacker reached an internal service and began sending out withdrawals that Binance never approved. The company said it found no sign of a stolen private key, the secret number that controls a wallet.

A day later, co-CEO Richard Teng made clear the laptop was only the start. The attacker went well beyond what one engineer could do, he said, and well beyond a single click: a longer, more involved process, with more than one point where he got in. Teng also said the attacker used software that wiped its own tracks while it worked, which made the attack harder to follow.

TRM Labs, which followed the money chain by chain, has a most likely read: the attacker got control of the system Binance uses to sign transactions, and made it sign whatever he asked. The keys themselves stayed put. Binance has not published its own root cause yet. Either way, the result was the same. Coins on ten different blockchains, each protected by a different kind of key, moved out with valid signatures inside the same half hour.

It also clears up something that looked like a contradiction. Binance says no key leaked, while a second security firm, Blockaid, counted eleven wallet keys signing the transfers. Both are right. The keys never left Binance’s own systems, and the machine that holds them signed on command.

On Ethereum the attacker used a feature that has only been around since May 2025.

It is called EIP-7702, and the idea behind it is friendly. It lets an ordinary wallet take on the powers of a smart contract, so it can do several things in one step or let someone else cover the transaction fee. To switch it on, the wallet owner signs once. That one signature can hand a contract full control of the wallet, and the control stays until the owner turns it off.

On a normal day it saves you time. In this attack it kept a Binance wallet under the attacker’s control after one signature.

At 20:20 UTC the attacker sent one transaction that carried 50 signed authorizations at once. Each one came from a Binance Ethereum hot wallet, known as Binance 14, and pointed it at a contract only he controlled. An authorization only works for one transaction number, and that number kept climbing because the wallet was busy handling withdrawals. By signing 50 numbers in a row, he made sure one would match the moment his transaction landed.

Three minutes and 24 seconds later, that wallet was empty. Gone in one sweep: 167,464 ETH, 63 different tokens, and 1.615 billion USDT. On the nine other chains he did not need the Ethereum trick; ordinary signed transfers moved the coins as fast.

The feature is a normal part of Ethereum now. EIP-7702 shipped as a regular upgrade, and plenty of legitimate wallets use it. But it has a side that security people warned about from the start. The same one-signature handover that makes a wallet easier to use is all a thief needs to empty it, and fake websites have been tricking people into signing it for months.

The same convenience is what let one signature drain a Binance wallet in a single move.

The money left in waves, and the order it left in shows how well prepared this was:

  • → 20:05 UTC: five XRP wallets sent 233 million XRP in four minutes
  • → shortly after 20:10 UTC: wallets on Solana and Optimism were emptied
  • → 20:20 UTC: a Bitcoin wallet sent 18,270 BTC, and a Tron wallet sent 612 million USDT
  • → 23:05 UTC: a second wave hit Avalanche and Polygon

None of this was improvised. The groundwork started more than a day before. The attacker began funding that wallet on October 28, in small amounts sent through Tornado Cash, a service built to hide where crypto came from. Early on the 29th he tried a first version of his draining code on two test wallets. Then he rehearsed the finished version on a third wallet and sent the test money back to himself, checking that it worked. About four hours later, that same code went onto a Binance hot wallet.

He rehearsed on throwaway wallets that afternoon and emptied Binance that evening.

Because the control stayed switched on, Binance’s own systems kept topping the wallet back up. One separate Binance smart account, never touched directly, still lost 823 million dollars in USDC, because it had standing permission to pay the wallet that was now hijacked. Circle froze that USDC soon after. Around 80 minutes after the first sweep, Binance’s own deposit-collection system swept another 204 million USDT into the hijacked wallet, but Tether had already frozen it, so the attacker got nothing from that batch.

Then came the race that decides how much ever comes back.

Much of what the attacker grabbed was stablecoins, coins like USDT and USDC that are run by companies and are always meant to be worth one dollar. Because a company runs them, that company can freeze the coins tied to a theft and make them useless to the thief. The attacker knew this, so he moved fast to get out of them.

He sold about 325 million USDT on decentralized exchanges and bought roughly 122,300 ETH with it before the issuers could react. With another wallet he put 60 million USDT into a lending service called Aave and borrowed about 19,760 ETH against it. Moving that fast came at a price: to offload the stablecoins he gave up somewhere between 10 and 26 percent of their value.

He was turning money that can be frozen into money that cannot.

It half worked. Tether froze 971 million USDT within the hour, and later said the total it had locked passed 1.567 billion. Circle froze 823 million USDC. Ripple, World Liberty Financial, and the group that governs the Arbitrum network added more, bringing the frozen total to around 2.7 billion dollars.

The stablecoin issuers moved faster than Binance did. Tether froze the main wallet at 21:01 UTC, more than an hour before Binance paused withdrawals. At 22:06 UTC it blacklisted the hijacked Binance 14 wallet outright, which also blocked Binance’s own transfers from that address. For the next hour Binance was racing the thief to pull out what it still could, and the attacker’s delegation came off only after midnight.

But the rest cannot be touched. More than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth about 2.4 billion, are plain Ether and Bitcoin. No company stands behind those two to freeze them, so that money is still sitting with the attacker.

Tracing where the rest went shows how this group launders money. On Tron, 300 million USDT went into a lending service called JustLend. He swapped another batch on open exchanges. The Ripple stablecoin moved in two hops, and part of it was sold off. The 18,270 Bitcoin were split through a short peel chain into 19 addresses, most holding 1,000 coins each, a known way to make the trail hard to follow. TRM expects the next stage to run through cross-chain bridges and brokers who turn crypto into cash.

If you had money on Binance that night, you did not lose it.

Binance says it is covering the losses out of its SAFU fund, an emergency fund it started in 2018, and out of its own money. It has set aside about 6.34 billion dollars to do it. It paused withdrawals for a while to rebuild the system that was abused.

The last question is who.

The firms that trace stolen crypto for a living point to the same group: TraderTraitor, a hacking team that works for the North Korean state, inside the group the industry calls Lazarus. TRM Labs calls it high confidence, Chainalysis its assessment, Elliptic likely. This is a familiar name. The FBI, the US cyber-defense agency CISA, and the US Treasury named it back in 2022, for doing exactly this kind of thing to crypto companies. The Treasury sanctioned Lazarus as far back as 2019, and the same team got the blame for that Bybit hack last year.

North Korea keeps showing up in these stories for a reason. Crypto theft has become one of the ways the country brings in hard currency while it sits under heavy sanctions, and TraderTraitor has spent years going after exchanges, trading firms, and people holding large amounts of coins.

For North Korea this is a revenue stream, run by professionals.

The money ties it to one more case. An independent investigator who goes by ZachXBT showed that funds from this theft and from a separate 388 million dollar hack of the Bitget exchange in late September ended up mixed at the same address. That points toward one team behind both, though the shared amount so far is small.

A word of caution here. Working out who did it is one of the hardest parts of this field. Addresses get reused, tools get shared, and a trail can be laid on purpose to point at the wrong people. Elliptic adds a detail of its own: the thief was slow to move the money, which let more than 2.6 billion be frozen, and that is not how North Korean crews usually work. No government has confirmed the attribution. What investigators can prove is how the attack worked and where the coins went. Binance itself has stayed silent on who did it, and in Teng’s words the investigation has not pinned it on any individual.

The lesson here is a quiet one. The blockchain did its job. What failed was everything around it: a compromised laptop, more than one way into Binance, a day and a half of quiet setup, and a wallet feature that millions of people now have switched on.

That last part is something you can check yourself. On a site like revoke.cash, or in your wallet’s own settings, a delegation shows up as code starting with ef0100. Spot a delegation you never put there, revoke it, and move your coins to a fresh address.

If you hold Ethereum, take two minutes today to check your wallet for a delegation you never set.

Seeing how attackers get that first foothold, through phishing and social engineering, is where ethical hacking begins.

The keys themselves stayed put. Binance has not published its own root cause yet. Either way, the result was the same. Coins on ten different blockchains, each protected by a different kind of key, moved out with valid signatures inside the same half hour.

It also clears up something that looked like a contradiction. Binance says no key leaked, while a second security firm, Blockaid, counted eleven wallet keys signing the transfers. Both are right. The keys never left Binance’s own systems, and the machine that holds them signed on command.

On Ethereum the attacker used a feature that has only been around since May 2025.

It is called EIP-7702, and the idea behind it is friendly. It lets an ordinary wallet take on the powers of a smart contract, so it can do several things in one step or let someone else cover the transaction fee. To switch it on, the wallet owner signs once. That one signature can hand a contract full control of the wallet, and the control stays until the owner turns it off.

On a normal day it saves you time. In this attack it kept a Binance wallet under the attacker’s control after one signature.

At 20:20 UTC the attacker sent one transaction that carried 50 signed authorizations at once. Each one came from a Binance Ethereum hot wallet, known as Binance 14, and pointed it at a contract only he controlled. An authorization only works for one transaction number, and that number kept climbing because the wallet was busy handling withdrawals. Three minutes and 24 seconds later, that wallet was empty. Gone in one sweep: 167,464 ETH, 63 different tokens, and 1.615 billion USDT. On the nine other chains he did not need the Ethereum trick; ordinary signed transfers moved the coins as fast.

The feature is a normal part of Ethereum now. EIP-7702 shipped as a regular upgrade, and plenty of legitimate wallets use it. But it has a side that security people warned about from the start. The same convenience is what let one signature drain a Binance wallet in a single move.

The money left in waves, and the order it left in shows how well prepared this was:

He was turning money that can be frozen into money that cannot.

The last question is who.

The firms that trace stolen crypto for a living point to the same group: TraderTraitor, a hacking team that works for the North Korean state, inside the group the industry calls Lazarus. North Korea keeps showing up in these stories for a reason. Crypto theft has become one of the ways the country brings in hard currency while it sits under heavy sanctions, and TraderTraitor has spent years going after exchanges, trading firms, and people holding large amounts of coins.

For North Korea this is a revenue stream, run by professionals.

item.title: Sign in with Google and How to Clean Up the Apps Connected to Your Accounts
item.description:
That little “Sign in with Google” button has quietly handed dozens of apps a way into your accounts, and changing your password does not lock most of them out. They were approved with one click, years ago, and never looked at again.

You know the button. It sits on one signup page after another, right under the empty username box. Sign in with Google. Or with Apple, Microsoft, Facebook, GitHub. You tap it, you pick the account you already have, and you are in, with no new password to invent and nothing to write down. It feels like the easy, safe choice, and usually it is.

Look at what you hand over when you tap it. You are telling that website to go ask Google who you are, and Google vouches for you. Your password never reaches the website. That part is good. The weak password you would have picked for some random forum, the one you reuse everywhere, never gets created, and one strong account with two-factor authentication stands in for all of them.

The trouble is that this one account is now the way into the rest. Your email, your files, your old shopping sites, that app you tried once and forgot: they all lean on Google to say you are you. So if someone gets into your Google account, your email is the least of it. They can walk straight into those other accounts too, with no extra password to crack.

A break-in is only one way this goes wrong. It can also go the other way. If Google, Apple or Facebook locks or suspends your account, for a rule you broke without knowing or a mistake on their side, the way into each service you signed in with stops working at the same moment. Your mail, your files, the shops, the tools, sometimes accounts with money attached, all shut at once, and you are left arguing with a support form to get any of it back. One account held it all, so one account can take it all away.

A quieter cost comes with it. Each time you use the button, Google notes that you did, and over the years that becomes a tidy picture of where you go: the shops, the forums, the tools, the apps you would rather keep to yourself. The button is handy, and it hands that running list straight to Google.

Two kinds of connected apps

Open the list of apps tied to your account and you will see a jumble. Some of them only use Google to log you in. That is it. They wave you through and touch nothing else. Others asked for more, and you said yes without thinking twice, because the screen went by fast.

That second kind is the one to watch. When you first connected it, a screen popped up listing what the app wanted. If it only asked for your name and email, that is a plain login. But if it asked to read your email, open your files, or post for you, and you tapped Allow, that app can now reach into your account whenever it likes, until you stop it.

Say you signed up for a photo app three years ago with Sign in with Google and let it into your Drive. If it has kept checking in since, it still reaches your files, and you have not thought about it once. One thing works in your favour: Google lets a connection’s access expire after six months without use, so a long-forgotten app may still sit in your list but no longer have working access. The ones still quietly syncing in the background are the ones that stay dangerous, especially if that company has since been sold or breached.

Here is a simple check for the next time that screen appears. Ask whether the app really needs what it is asking for. A game has no reason to read your Gmail. A photo filter has no reason to see your contacts. If the request is bigger than the job, that is your cue to back out instead of tapping Allow.

Three things that feel safe but do nothing

This is where clean-ups usually go wrong. You do the obvious thing, feel safer, and the connection is still sitting there wide open, because the obvious thing never touched it. These three come up again and again.

Changing your password barely helps. The app runs on a separate token, a long code that stands in for you, and it holds on to that code regardless of your password. A new password only cuts off apps that can read your Gmail; the sign-in links and the apps that reach your Drive, calendar or contacts keep right on working.

Deleting the app off your phone does not help either. That permission sits in your Google or Apple account, up on their servers, not in the app on your phone. Delete the app and the account still lets it in.

Removing a connection does not wipe what the app already took. Cut its access today and it stops getting anything new, but whatever it already copied is still sitting on its servers. For that you have to open the app itself and delete your account there.

If that sounds theoretical, it is not. On 1 September 2026 the FBI put out a warning about an attack called consent phishing. Someone sets up a legitimate-looking app, sends you a link, and you land on a genuine Google or Microsoft screen asking you to Allow. You tap it, thinking it is normal. No password is ever stolen, because the attacker does not need one.

The FBI spelled out the hard part: once you have tapped Allow, changing your password will not get rid of them. The access “can only be revoked by the victim invalidating the token in their application security settings.” In other words, you have to go into the list and pull it out by hand.

What to do, step by step

Cleaning this up takes about fifteen minutes, and you only have to do it properly once. Here is where to go.

One thing to sort out before you start pulling links. If a site only ever let you in through Sign in with Google, and you never set a password for it, then the moment you remove that link you are locked out of your own account there. So for anything you still want to keep, open that site first, set a password or add a second way to log in, and only then cut the Google connection. For the stuff you are done with, pull it and move on.

Start with Google, since that is the big one.

  • → Open myaccount.google.com/linkedapps on your phone or laptop.
  • → Tap the filter that says “Sign in with Google” to see the sites you log into this way.
  • → Tap one, open See details, and choose Stop using Sign in with Google. Do that for anything you do not recognize or have not used in a year.
  • → Then switch the filter to “Access to your Google Account.” These apps can read your data, so be stricter here. Tap any you do not trust and choose Remove access.

The rest work the same way, in a different spot.

  • → Apple: on your iPhone, open Settings, tap your name at the top, then Sign in with Apple. On a computer, go to account.apple.com and look under Sign-In and Security. Tap an app and choose to stop using it.
  • → Microsoft: go to account.microsoft.com, open Privacy, and find the apps and services that can access your data (the direct link is microsoft.com/consent). Pick the app and remove its permissions.
  • → GitHub: go to Settings, then Applications, then Authorized OAuth Apps. Tap anything old or unfamiliar and choose Revoke. One heads-up: on GitHub this also removes any keys the app set up for you, so check before you clear a tool you still use.
  • → Facebook: open Settings and privacy, then Settings, then Apps and websites. Tap an app and choose Remove.

Do not worry if the list is longer than you expected. Work from the top, and when you are unsure about something, remove it. You can always reconnect it later with one tap if it turns out you need it. Keep the handful of apps you actually use, pull anything you do not recognize, and if you spot one you never signed up for, remove it and then check your recent sign-ins for anything odd.

And do one more thing while you are in there. Because this account is now the way into the rest, protect it as well as you can: turn on two-factor authentication, and add a passkey if the account offers one. That guards against a stolen password. It will not stop the consent-phishing trick above, though: once you tap Allow yourself, no second step stands in the way.

This is the single best habit here, and the part the step-by-step guides almost always skip. Stop giving out your main email address. When a site asks for it, hand over an alias instead: a stand-in address that forwards to your inbox without being your inbox, a different one for each site. If that site is breached, or quietly sells its list, the spam and the scams land on an address you can switch off in a second, and it never points back to the account that holds your mail, your photos and your logins.

Setting one up is quick, and free to start. The simplest route is Proton Mail. (That Proton link is an affiliate link: it supports this site, and signing up through it gets you a discount.)

  • → Make a Proton account, then open mail.proton.me and click the shield icon, the Security center, on the right.
  • → Open Hide-my-email aliases and click New alias.
  • → Click Create and copy alias. That address is now on your clipboard, ready to paste into the signup form.

Install the Proton Pass browser extension and it gets easier still: when a signup page asks for your email, click the field, choose Hide my email, and it makes a fresh alias and fills it in for you. On an iPhone you already have a version of this: Sign in with Apple can hand a site a hidden, forwarding address for free, and Apple’s Hide My Email (part of iCloud+) lets you create your own one-off addresses on top of that.

Two things to know before you lean on this. Some free aliases can only receive mail, not send a reply, which is awkward when a shop needs to write back about an order, so pick one that can reply both ways. And because the alias service passes your mail through its own servers, pick one that states in writing that it does not read it. Proton, Apple and Firefox all say so.

If you want to go a step further, look at passkeys. Instead of a password, your phone keeps a private key and proves it is you with your fingerprint or face, so it cannot be typed into a fake page or reused somewhere else. And for your most important accounts, your main email and anything tied to money, think twice before using the button at all: a password in a password manager, or a passkey, keeps those off the one account the rest relies on.

You do not have to swear off the button. It fixed a genuine problem, and logging in with one guarded account is safer than scattering weak passwords across the web. The win is knowing what is tied to you, clearing out the apps and sites you left behind, and keeping the list short enough to recognize at a glance. The ones you use stay, and the forgotten ones are gone.

Cleaning this up is the easy half; the harder half is understanding how attackers find and exploit accounts like these in the first place.

My Ethical Hacking Complete Course Zero to Expert takes you there step by step: reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation and traffic analysis, hands-on, from your first day with no Linux or hacking background.

FBI IC3 PSA I-090126-PSA | Google Identity: OAuth 2.0 token expiration | Google Account Help: manage links to third-party apps | Apple Support: Sign in with Apple & Hide My Email

item.title: Microsoft Edge Hacked With Logic Bugs Only in a $175,000 Pwn2Own Chain
item.description:
A single web page took over a fully patched Windows computer straight through Microsoft Edge, and the break-in paid 175,000 dollars at a hacking contest. The person who got hit only opened the page. The break-in chained 5 flaws with 2 built-in Windows features and no memory bug at all; the features worked as built, and the holes sat in the checks around them.

The page asked for no download and no file to run, and the browser never crashed. It loaded the way a page loads, and by the time it finished, code chosen by the attacker was running on the machine with the same rights as the person in front of it.

This was done in the open at Pwn2Own Berlin, the contest where researchers attack fully updated software in front of a room and get paid for each break-in that lands. The Edge attack paid 175,000 dollars. The payout drew the headlines, but the method is what made it strange, because the attack ran on logic from the first step to the last, with no memory corruption at any point.

That difference is the heart of it. Almost always, breaking out of a browser has meant finding a memory bug. That is a spot where the program gets pushed into writing data where it does not belong, so an attacker can wedge in their own instructions. Browsers are built with layer on layer to stop exactly that. A logic flaw works another way. Nothing overflows and nothing gets corrupted. Each part does the ordinary thing it was written to do, and the attacker only arranges those ordinary things into an order the designers never planned for. The memory defenses have nothing to catch, because on paper the software behaved.

The holes sat in one place. Edge is built on Chromium, the same engine under Google Chrome, and that engine’s own guardrails mostly held. The weak spots were in what Microsoft bolted on top to make Edge friendlier and more useful for companies: a helper that steers work accounts to the right profile, an automatic sign-in, its own reading mode, its own list of sites allowed to pop up a window. The parts that made Edge convenient were the parts that gave way, one after another.

A feature called OneAuth then signs that account in automatically on Microsoft’s own sites. Edge is then signed in to a Microsoft identity as soon as someone opens a Microsoft site.

A machine can be taken over without being broken, talked into a chain of reasonable things in an order that no sensible person would choose.

item.title: Ubuntu Servers Still Wait for a Fix to a 9.8 Linux Kernel Bug That an AI Turned Into a Root Exploit
item.description:
Linux servers on Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 are 18 days behind Debian on a 9.8 kernel bug. 53 minutes, no password, and a server runs commands as root. An AI wrote that exploit, for a flaw that has sat in Linux TCP since 2016.

On November 3, Ubuntu’s own security page for CVE-2026-98432 still lists Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 as Vulnerable, with a short note that work is in progress. The Linux kernel developers released the fix on October 15, and Debian shipped it to its users the next day. SUSE began releasing updates on October 29. Red Hat, which rates the bug Critical, the highest level on its scale, followed on November 1 for its Enterprise Linux 8, 9 and 10. The three Ubuntu versions still waiting are its long-term support releases, the releases built to run on a server for years, with five years of security updates by default.

The score of 9.8 out of 10 comes from the Linux kernel’s own CVE team. It means the bug can be reached over the network, without an account or a password, and without a person on the server clicking or opening anything.

The flaw came to light through Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models. In a research post published on October 27, its Frontier Red Team wrote that it found the bug with an AI model that has not been released to the public. After a first prompt from the team, the AI wrote a working exploit for it.

That exploit sends packets to a Linux server that has a Multipath TCP listener open. It ends with a shell command of the attacker’s choice running as root, with no login and no action needed on the server’s side. In their test it took 48 minutes to pull a kernel pointer out of the target, and about five more minutes to get the command to run. On the kernel side, the fix names Xinyang Ge, with an anthropic.com address, as the person who reported it.

To see why this works, start with the way a TCP connection opens. A computer that wants to talk to a server sends a small packet called a SYN. The server answers with a SYN-ACK, the computer sends an ACK back, and the connection is open. This is the three-way handshake, and it happens before a server sends back a single web page or login screen. An IPv4 packet can also carry a few extra fields in its header, called IP options, up to 40 bytes of them. When a SYN arrives with options attached, Linux keeps a copy of those options and echoes them back to the sender inside its SYN-ACK.

The trouble starts when the same SYN arrives twice, which is normal on the internet, because a client that hears nothing back in time simply sends its SYN again. A second processor core can then begin building a fresh SYN-ACK from those stored options, while the first core finishes setting up the connection and hands the options over to the new connection without copying them. When that new connection is freed, the options are freed with it, and the second core can still be reading from memory that no longer belongs to the connection. By then the kernel may already have handed that memory to something else.

When the result depends on which of two cores gets there first, that is called a race condition, and here it ends in a use-after-free, right in the code that answers incoming connections, on any port where a server listens.

In the first stage of the exploit, the race makes the kernel read a length field that the attacker controls. The kernel then copies extra bytes into its reply and sends them out, and among them is a kernel pointer, an address that shows where the kernel sits in memory. Linux shuffles that layout each time it starts, a protection called KASLR, so a remote attacker cannot predict it, and one leaked pointer is enough to undo it.

In the second stage, the same use-after-free is used to overwrite a callback pointer, an address the kernel will later jump to, so that it points at a payload the attacker staged earlier. That payload strings together functions that already exist inside the kernel, and the last of them runs the attacker’s shell command as root.

A race like this does not succeed on the first try, and that is where the 48 minutes come from. A lost attempt only breaks that one handshake, without crashing the server, so the attacker can keep sending attempts until one succeeds. The race also makes the attack harder to pull off than the score alone suggests. SUSE scores it 8.1 instead of 9.8, because it rates the attack complexity as high, and Red Hat writes that reliable code execution needs precise control over the kernel heap, the memory the kernel hands out while it runs.

The code change behind this bug is more than ten years old. On October 2, 2015, Eric Dumazet changed the way Linux stores incoming connection requests, so that they sit in the main lookup table while the handshake is still going on. That change shipped in Linux 4.4, released on January 10, 2016, and the kernels released since then carry the flaw. A second path into the same bug arrived in June 2021, through a feature that moves waiting connection requests from one listening socket to another. That feature is turned off by default.

Eleven years after the original change, on October 1, 2026, the same man wrote the fix. The engineer who added the second path in 2021 reviewed it. The patch itself is small: where the kernel used to free the stored options straight away, it now waits until no other processor core can still be reading them, using a method called RCU, which stands for read-copy-update. The options stay in memory for that short window, and only then does the kernel release them.

Multipath TCP, or MPTCP, is a version of TCP that lets one connection run over several network paths at the same time, for example over a wired link and a mobile link together. The exploit from the red team needs a server with an MPTCP listener. Ubuntu builds MPTCP into its 24.04 kernel on all supported architectures, and the Linux kernel turns it on by default.

On top of that, since Go 1.24, released in February 2025, programs written in Go open their listening sockets on Linux with MPTCP by default. A server program built with a recent version of Go, such as the Caddy web server, can therefore be listening with MPTCP on a stock Ubuntu 24.04 kernel without its administrator ever choosing it. The Go security team sent out a warning about exactly this on October 29.

Switching MPTCP off closes the route this one exploit takes, and the flaw itself stays in plain IPv4 TCP. A Red Hat security bulletin states that MPTCP is not required for the bug, and that OpenShift nodes, where MPTCP is disabled, are still affected. Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu, writes that the fix is not specific to MPTCP.

The reason Ubuntu is behind comes down to which kernel each distribution runs. Debian runs on the 6.12 kernel line, which received the fix in version 6.12.113 on October 15, so Debian only had to package it. Ubuntu 22.04 runs on its own build of the 5.15 line, and 5.15.223 with the fix came out on that same October 15. Ubuntu 24.04 runs on 6.8 and Ubuntu 26.04 on 7.0. The fix from the kernel developers did not come out for those two lines, so the Ubuntu kernel team has to carry it over itself.

That work is done: fixed kernels for 22.04 and 24.04 went into a section of the Ubuntu archive called -proposed on October 26, and the kernel for 26.04 followed on October 28. The -proposed pocket is Ubuntu’s testing area. Packages there are not picked up by a normal update, so a server only receives them when its administrator turns that pocket on by hand. In a blog post on November 2, Ubuntu wrote that the kernels are in qualification testing on more than 2,000 certified servers and devices. They move to the regular updates as soon as those tests are complete, and the post gives no date.

The same blog post describes the CVSS score of 9.8 as a severity of High, one step below Critical. The Ubuntu Server page promises timely patches for critical vulnerabilities to customers of Ubuntu Pro, the paid subscription. The older releases, Ubuntu 20.04, 18.04 and 16.04, only receive security fixes through that subscription, and all three are still listed as fix pending.

An Ubuntu server can be checked in a minute. The first command shows which kernel is running, the second lists the kernel packages that are installed:

1
2

uname -r
dpkg -l 'linux-image*' | grep ^ii

Two more commands show whether a server matches the setup of the published exploit. The first prints 1 when MPTCP is switched on, the second lists the listening sockets that use it, with the program behind each one:

1
2

sysctl net.mptcp.enabled
sudo ss -lnMp

For administrators who want the fixed kernel from the testing pocket now instead of waiting, Ubuntu gives these commands, and says this route is meant for teams that test kernels themselves before rolling them out. They turn on the -proposed pocket and install the kernel from it, and the server needs a restart afterwards. The install line assumes a kernel that was installed through a meta-package:

1
2
3
4

sudo add-apt-repository --component main --pocket proposed http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu
sudo apt update
dpkg-query -W -f '${source:Package}\t${binary:Package}\n' | awk '$1 ~ "^linux-meta" { print $2 }' | xargs sudo apt install -t $(. /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME)-proposed --only-upgrade
sudo reboot

For servers that cannot take that step yet, the same bulletin publishes a firewall rule that drops incoming IPv4 TCP packets with IP options, so the bug never gets its input. Save it as cve-2026-98432.nft:

1
2
3
4
5
6

table inet cve_2026_98432 {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority -310; policy accept;
        ip protocol tcp ip hdrlength > 5 counter drop
    }
}

Then test the file and load it, and the last command confirms the table is active:

1
2
3

sudo nft --check --file cve-2026-98432.nft
sudo nft --file cve-2026-98432.nft
sudo nft list table inet cve_2026_98432

The rule has limits, and Ubuntu’s own CVE page spells them out:

  • → It covers the host itself, and containers with their own network setup need the rule applied separately
  • → It is gone after a reboot unless it is added to /etc/nftables.conf
  • → It breaks connections that depend on IPv4 options, such as CIPSO security labels
  • → IPv6 traffic does not need it, because IPv6 is not affected by the main bug

The bulletin calls the rule a way to reduce exposure and not a replacement for the kernel update. Ubuntu’s security team goes further and says the update itself is the only proper fix. Once the fixed kernel is running, the rule comes off again with sudo nft delete table inet cve_2026_98432.

So far there is no report of this bug being used in a successful attack, but the scanning has started. Security researcher Marcus Hutchins wrote on November 3 that a scan on October 30 found about 2.1 million servers reachable over MPTCP on port 443, without showing which of them are patched. Since November 2 his team has seen residential proxies and Russia-based VPN servers probing port 443 with MPTCP, which ordinary scanners do not use, and he suspects attackers looking for this bug. Denial-of-service proof-of-concepts are already circulating, and the exploit from the red team has not been released.

The CVE does not appear in the list of known exploited vulnerabilities kept by CISA, the US cybersecurity agency. Debian already has a fixed kernel, and so do the standard kernels of Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9 and 10, while SUSE has fixes out for several of its versions with others still in progress. On those systems the fix only takes effect after the update and a reboot, when uname -r shows the new version.

On Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04, a plain sudo apt upgrade will not bring in the fix until it moves out of -proposed. A server there that reports nothing left to update can still be running the vulnerable kernel today.

The SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK at the center of this bug are packets you can capture and read yourself on your own network with Wireshark.
